theory.intro: The **reverse chain rule** undoes the chain rule. When the derivative of the inner function appears as a factor, $\int f'(x)\left[f(x)\right]^{n}dx = \dfrac{\left[f(x)\right]^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$ for $n \ne -1$. Without that factor the method does not apply.
facts: The **inner function** $f(x)$ is the expression inside the bracket that is raised to the power $n$.
Increase the power of the bracket by one and divide by the new power, leaving the bracket itself unchanged.
The factor $f'(x)$ must be present, so $\int\left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{3}dx$ cannot be done by this method.
A constant multiple of $f'(x)$ is enough: divide by that constant at the end.
For a linear inner function, $f'(x) = a$, giving $\int(ax + b)^{n}dx = \dfrac{(ax + b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)} + C$.
The rule also covers negative and fractional powers, such as $\int f'(x)\sqrt{f(x)}\,dx$.
Check any answer by differentiating it with the chain rule.
For a definite integral, evaluate $\left[\dfrac{\left[f(x)\right]^{n+1}}{n+1}\right]_{a}^{b}$ without changing the limits.
steps: Choose the inner function $f(x)$ and differentiate it to get $f'(x)$.
Check that $f'(x)$ appears as a factor, up to a constant multiple.
Raise the power of the bracket by one and divide by the new power.
Divide by whatever constant is needed so that differentiating back gives the integrand.

foundation.question_text: For $\int 3x^{2}\left(x^{3} - 7\right)^{5}dx$, state the inner function $f(x)$ and its derivative $f'(x)$.
foundation.solution_text:
$f(x) = x^{3} - 7$
$f'(x) = 3x^{2}$
The factor $3x^{2}$ in the integral is exactly $f'(x)$.

foundation.question_text: Explain why the reverse chain rule cannot be used to find $\int\left(x^{2} + 3\right)^{4}dx$.
foundation.solution_text:
The inner function is $f(x) = x^{2} + 3$, so $f'(x) = 2x$.
The integrand has no factor of $2x$, nor any constant multiple of it.
The method needs $f'(x)$ present, so it does not apply here.

development.solution_text:
$f(x) = 4 - x^{3}$, so $f'(x) = -3x^{2}$.
$\int x^{2}\left(4 - x^{3}\right)^{7}dx$
$= -\dfrac{1}{3}\int \left(-3x^{2}\right)\left(4 - x^{3}\right)^{7}dx$
$= -\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{\left(4 - x^{3}\right)^{8}}{8} + C$
$= -\dfrac{\left(4 - x^{3}\right)^{8}}{24} + C$

development.question_text:
Only one of these integrals can be found with the reverse chain rule. Identify it and name the inner function.
A. $\int\left(x^{2} - 9\right)^{5}dx$
B. $\int x^{3}\left(x^{2} - 9\right)^{5}dx$
C. $\int 4x\left(x^{2} - 9\right)^{5}dx$
development.solution_text:
In each integral the inner function is $f(x) = x^{2} - 9$, so $f'(x) = 2x$.
A has no factor of $x$ at all.
B has the factor $x^{3}$, which is not a constant multiple of $2x$.
C has the factor $4x = 2(2x)$, a constant multiple of $f'(x)$, so only C can be done this way.

mastery.question_text: Show that $\int\left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}dx$ cannot be found by the reverse chain rule, then find it another way.
mastery.solution_text:
The inner function is $f(x) = x^{2} + 1$, so $f'(x) = 2x$.
The integrand has no factor of $2x$, so the reverse chain rule does not apply.
$\int\left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}dx$
$= \int\left(x^{4} + 2x^{2} + 1\right)dx$
$= \dfrac{x^{5}}{5} + \dfrac{2x^{3}}{3} + x + C$
